executive_summary: The dominant thread running through today's content is the Trump administration's aggressive use of political and legal power to reshape both domestic opposition and U.S. foreign policy simultaneously. On the domestic front, the primary defeat of Rep. Thomas Massie by a Trump-backed challenger signals the near-complete consolidation of MAGA loyalty within the Republican Party, while the Justice Department's charges against Raúl Castro and Trump's push toward a Cuba endgame reflect a broader, coordinated hemispheric strategy that also encompasses the administration's posture on Mexico's cartels and its maneuvering around Iran and Ukraine. The Economist's warning that the 'MAGA tax' is holding America back economically provides the critical connective tissue: what looks like bold geopolitical assertion carries a compounding domestic cost in investor confidence, institutional stability, and global standing. Together, the newsletters and breaking news paint a portrait of an administration that is winning internal political battles while potentially mortgaging long-term American credibility and economic health to do so. This tension — between short-term political dominance and long-term strategic cost — is the story that will define the months ahead.

newsletters.title: 🔴 The Insider: The MAGA tax is holding America back

items.headline: The MAGA tax is holding America back
items.blurb: For the past year America has been running a giant experiment. What happens when you take one of the world's most successful economies and put in place two big growth-busting changes: tariffs and a sudden stop in immigration? Many observers—including us—thought the impact would be unambiguously negative. Yet America's economy is still the envy of the rich world. The country's GDP grew faster than that of any other G7 country last year. Its stockmarkets have repeatedly hit record highs over the past 15 months. We have crunched the numbers. An artificial-intelligence boom, soaring stockmarkets and some of Donald Trump's own measures have boosted the economy. But by our calculations, the president's chaotic policymaking, sweeping tariffs and mass deportations are, in fact, hurting growth—a drag we call the "MAGA tax". Our calculations suggest that without the MAGA tax, America's economy would have grown more than half a percentage point faster.

newsletters.title: The Evening: U.S. charges Raúl Castro

items.headline: The U.S. charges Raúl Castro, increasing the pressure on Cuba
items.blurb:
The Justice Department charged Raúl Castro, the 94-year-old former president of Cuba and brother of Fidel Castro, with murder and a conspiracy to kill U.S. citizens. The accusations stem from the 1996 downing of two civilian planes, which were connected to a group that made provocative flights over the island.
The charges, which can be read here, are part of an effort by the Trump administration to topple Cuba's Communist government. They also laid the grounds for potential action by the U.S. military to remove Raúl Castro from the country. American officials used an indictment of Venezuela's former leader, Nicolás Maduro, as reason to capture him in Caracas and to reshape the country's government.
Castro is frail, has poor hearing and difficulty speaking and no longer holds any official title, but he still wields enormous power, particularly over the military. He has also had a hand in secret negotiations with the Trump administration.
Months ago, Marco Rubio, the secretary of state and the son of immigrants who left Cuba before the Castro revolution, reached out to a grandson of Castro to try to negotiate an economic opening. But U.S. officials have grown impatient. In a rare direct address, Rubio urged Cubans to align with the Trump administration. Cuba's ambassador to the U.N. said the country was ready to negotiate, but did not believe the U.S. was operating in good faith.

items.headline: Jan. 6 police officers sue to block Trump's new fund
items.blurb:
Two police officers who defended the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, filed a lawsuit today in an effort to block a $1.8 billion fund created this week by the Justice Department to pay people who claim mistreatment by the federal government.
The officers accused the Trump administration of creating a "slush fund" to reward the pro-Trump rioters who had tried to stop the certification of the 2020 election. Multiple Jan. 6 rioters have expressed excitement about the prospect of getting paid.
The arrangement between President Trump and his own administration — including the fund and a guarantee of immunity from I.R.S. audits — has generated widespread opposition and raised profound questions about presidential power. The whole enterprise, our chief legal correspondent writes, tests the limits of the America's constitutional system.

items.headline: The U.S. and Israel aimed to install a hard-liner in Iran
items.blurb:
At the start of the Iran war, the U.S. and Israel had an audacious and surprising plan: They wanted to replace Iran's supreme leader with Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, a former Iranian president known for his anti-Israel and anti-American views.
The plan, which Ahmadinejad was consulted on, quickly went awry: Ahmadinejad was wounded in a strike that had been designed to free him from house arrest. Soon after, he became disillusioned with the regime-change effort and has not been seen since.

newsletters.title: Colossal Biosciences is growing chickens in a 3D-printed artificial eggshell

items.headline: Colossal Biosciences is growing chickens in a 3D-printed artificial eggshell
items.blurb:
The baby chicks were shifting and starting to pip—or trying to hatch. But not from an egg. Instead, these chickens were growing inside transparent 3D-printed plastic cups at the Dallas headquarters of Colossal Biosciences.

The biotech company yesterday claimed it has developed a "fully artificial egg" as part of its effort to resurrect extinct avian species, including birds like the dodo and the giant moa.

Some scientists think Colossal is overstating the breakthrough. But the technology may represent an early step toward artificial wombs.

items.headline: Inside the Musk v. Altman Trial
items.blurb:
Elon Musk has lost his landmark lawsuit against OpenAI, which centered on allegations that its cofounders Sam Altman and Greg Brockman misled him about the company's nonprofit mission. But what really happened in the courtroom, and what does it mean for the AI race?

AI reporter and attorney Michelle Kim, who covered the trial for MIT Technology Review, joined our editor in chief Mat Honan to unpack it all in an exclusive Roundtables discussion yesterday.

items.headline: MIT Technology Review Narrated: this scientist rewarmed and studied pieces of his friend's cryopreserved brain
items.blurb:
L. Stephen Coles's brain sits in a vat at a storage facility in Arizona. It has been held there at a temperature of around −146 degrees °C for over a decade, largely undisturbed. Before he died in 2014, Coles had the brain frozen with an ambitious goal in mind: reanimation.

His friend, cryobiologist Greg Fahy, believes it could be revived one day. But other experts are less optimistic.

Still, Fahy's research could lead to new ways to study the brain. And using cryopreservation for organ transplantation is becoming a viable reality.

items.headline: Can AI learn to understand the world?
items.blurb:
The limitations of LLMs are pushing AI researchers towards new systems that understand the physical environment: world models. The likes of Google DeepMind, Fei-Fei Li's World Labs, and Meta's former Chief AI Scientist, AI Yann LeCun, have brought this technology to the forefront of AI.

To explore where this technology is heading next, MIT Technology Review is hosting an exclusive Roundtables discussion on Thursday, May 21, with editor in chief Mat Honan, senior AI editor Will Douglas Heaven, and AI reporter Grace Huckins.

longform.title: 8 Atlantic stories worth returning to
longform.thesis: Certain long-form journalism transcends the news cycle and retains lasting analytical and emotional relevance, as demonstrated by eight Atlantic articles that readers have repeatedly returned to across years.
longform.context: This is a curated editorial email from The Atlantic, published May 2026, compiling reader-favorite longform articles from recent years as evergreen reading recommendations — not a single article but a digest prompt pointing to eight distinct pieces.
arguments: Personal narratives about systemic injustice — Alex Tizon's 'My Family's Slave' and Ta-Nehisi Coates's 'The Case for Reparations' — endure because they force reckoning with moral debts that remain unresolved, using intimate or historical evidence to make structural arguments visceral.

Pieces diagnosing social and psychological conditions — Jennifer Senior on adult friendship loss, Arthur C. Brooks on desire and satisfaction, Anne-Marie Slaughter on structural barriers to gender equality — remain relevant because the conditions they describe are persistent features of modern life, not episodic crises.

Investigative and data-driven pieces — William Langewiesche on MH370 and Sarah Zhang on DNA-revealed incest prevalence — retain readership by exposing institutional concealment or taboo realities that mainstream coverage avoids, suggesting that suppressed or uncomfortable truth is itself a driver of long-term engagement.

Jonathan Haidt's argument that 'the past 10 years of American life have been uniquely stupid' and that 'it's not just a phase' frames social media-era cultural fragmentation as structural and durable, which has only gained explanatory power as the conditions he diagnosed have intensified.
longform.significance: The selection reveals what Atlantic readers treat as intellectually durable: pieces that name a structural condition, carry moral weight, or uncover concealed truth rather than merely report events. The curation implicitly argues that journalism's highest value lies not in timeliness but in explanatory staying power. In a media environment dominated by ephemeral content, this list functions as a counter-programming statement about depth over velocity.
questions_raised: The piece asserts these articles 'live beyond the news cycle' but provides no methodology for how 'most-loved' was determined — raising the question of whether durability reflects genuine intellectual value or algorithmic and demographic skew in The Atlantic's subscriber base.

The list is heavily weighted toward American social pathologies and elite anxieties; whether this reflects the universal human concerns the framing implies, or the specific preoccupations of a particular readership, remains unexamined.
